newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico peace group wants EPR rebels in talks.
newsitem.headline: Mexico peace group wants EPR rebels in talks.

text.p: A broad coalition of peace groups led by mediators between the Mexican government and Zapatista rebels on Tuesday sought inclusion of a new and more violent guerrilla force in peace negotiations.

The group said the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), a recently emerged rebel force in southern Mexico, should be included in a "national dialogue" aimed at stemming the alarming rise of violence in Mexico in recent months.

The initiative was presented at a news conference led by Roman Catholic Bishop Samuel Ruiz Garcia, president of the National Mediation Commission (CONAI), which is attempting to broker peace between the Zapatistas and the government.

The Zapatistas launched an uprising in January 1994 in the southeastern state of Chiapas, and have been in on-off peace talks with the government since. The EPR emerged in June and has not yet appeared keen to talk.

In seeking to underscore differences between the two groups, the Mexican government has spoken warmly of the Zapatistas, while it has labelled the apparently unrelated EPR as "terrorist" and has refused to negotiate with it.

But its efforts to broker a peace accord with the Zapatistas has been undermined by the EPR rebellion. After the EPR launched a series of strikes against police and military units in August, the Zapatistas unilaterally suspended the Chiapas peace talks.
The call for nationwide peace talks came from some 457 peace groups and prominent activists, and appeared aimed at the government, the army, the EPR and the Zapatistas.

In the past, the government has been deaf to calls for national peace talks, however. It has constantly resisted efforts by the Zapatistas to broaden talks to cover issues of national scope, saying they should be limited to Chiapas, the only state where the Zapatistas have a significent presence.
The peace initiative presented on Tuesday called on the Mexican army to scale back troop movements in Chiapas that have drawn a storm of protest from the Zapatistas.
It also demanded that the government enact profound political reforms. Mexico has been ruled by a single force, the Institutional Revolutionary Party, for the last 67 years.
